caveats: tamserve không phải là NVR hoàn chỉnh như Frigate: nó không có giao diện web UI, không tự kết nối RTSP, không quản lý lưu trữ video 24/7 hay tích hợp Home Assistant sẵn.
Khởi động chế độ biên dịch tối ưu (compile=True) lần đầu mất rất nhiều thời gian (lên tới 1.190 giây trên RTX 4090) để compile các batch size và độ dài memory.
SAM 3 tương đối nặng và chậm (khoảng 65 ms cho một frame trên RTX 4090) nên phải dùng chiến thuật giãn cách 3 frame/lần để phối hợp cùng EdgeTAM.
Chạy trên CPU khả dụng nhưng quá chậm để xử lý video trực tiếp thời gian thực.

## aryamandarda/tamserve (https://github.com/aryamandarda/tamserve)
Description: Live, multi-camera object tracking with SAM3, SAM 2 and EdgeTAM, on one GPU or many. One model per GPU serves every camera: faster than the original code, about 4x less GPU memory, the same accuracy.

Latest release: v0.3.3 (2026-11-19)
README (start):
# tamserve

**Live, multi-camera tracking with SAM 2, on one GPU or many.**

SAM 2 and its smaller sibling EdgeTAM can track anything you point at, but their code was written for one recorded video at a time.
tamserve is the serving engine they are missing: one copy of the model tracks every object on every camera, for as long as the cameras run.
Point at what to track, or name it ("dog", "the red mug") and tamserve finds it.

[](https://colab.research.google.com/github/aryamandarda/tamserve/blob/main/notebooks/quickstart.ipynb)

[Why tamserve](#why-tamserve) · [New to video tracking?](#new-to-video-tracking) · [Using it](#using-it) · [Tracking by name](#following-what-you-name) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Results](#results) · [Limits](#limits)

Six live cameras on one GPU, every one at 30 frames/s. Watch the 32-second demo, or read how it was recorded.

## Why tamserve

The models are excellent. The code that comes with them was made for editing one recorded video, and the usual way to put it on several cameras is to run a separate copy of the model for each one. Memory piles up with every copy and with every minute of video.

tamserve does what LLM servers such as vLLM do for chat: every camera shares one copy of the model, and whatever needs the GPU at a given moment goes through it together. That turns out to be faster as well as lighter, and because the model itself is not touched, it is just as accurate.

| | the model's own code | tamserve |
|---|---|---|
| Several cameras | one copy of the model per camera | one copy for all of them |
| GPU memory, 8 cameras | 8.6 GB | 2.2 GB |
| Speed, 1 camera | 177 frames/s | 219 frames/s |
| Speed, 8 cameras | 280 frames/s | 323 frames/s |
| 64 cameras | would need about 70 GB of GPU memory | 321 frames/s in 5.7 GB |
| GPU memory for an 800-frame video | 9.8 GB | 0.28 GB, however long it runs |
| Starting to track something new mid-stream | not possible | on any frame |
| Finding what to track | you point at each object | you point, or you name it and a `Tracker` finds and follows every match by itself |
| Several GPUs | you split the cameras between them by hand | a `Router` places the cameras and gathers every result |
| Accuracy on DAVIS 2017 | 0.8686 | 0.8685 |

These are for EdgeTAM on one RTX 4090, against EdgeTAM's own code at its fastest: compiled, one copy per camera, all sharing the GPU. Speeds are totals across the cameras, with one object each. With the larger SAM 2.1 models, tamserve runs at the same speed as Meta's current SAM 2 code and uses about a third of the GPU memory. [Results](https://github.com/aryamandarda/tamserve/blob/main/docs/results.md) has the full tables.

## New to video tracking?

Say you have video, and you need to know where one particular thing is in every frame: this person, that forklift, the dog. That is tracking. SAM 2 and its smaller relatives, EdgeTAM and SAM 2.1, are models from Meta that do it very well. You point at the thing once, on a single frame, and the model draws its exact outline on every frame after that.

tamserve sits between one of those models and your program. Your program hands it the latest frame from each camera and gets back the outline of every tracked object in each one. You can start tracking something new, or stop, at any moment, and cameras can come and go.

It is meant for anyone who has to answer "where exactly is this thing, right now, in each of my video feeds": sports and broadcast graphics, warehouse and retail analytics, robotics, wildlife and lab monitoring, annotation tools.

There are two ways to say what to track. You can point: a person clicking on the picture, or a detector, says where the thing is, and tamserve takes over from there. Or you can name it: a [`Tracker`](#following-what-you-name) takes a word or a phrase, finds everything that matches on every camera, and follows it.

Four words come up a lot below:

| word | what it means here |
|---|---|
| frame | one image from a video |
| mask | the answer for one object in one frame: a grid of True and False the size of the frame, True on every pixel that belongs to the object |
| prompt | how you say what to track: a box around it, a click on it, a rough mask of it, or, with a `Tracker`, a word or a phrase |
| stock | the model's own code: the tracker in Meta's EdgeTAM repository, used exactly as it comes |

## Using it

### Install

```bash
pip install tamserve
```

You need Python 3.10 or newer and an NVIDIA GPU. It does run on a CPU, which is handy for trying it out but much too slow for live video. Tracking by name needs `pip install "tamserve[sam3]"` and Meta's SAM 3, as [described below](#following-what-you-name).

The first time you load a model, tamserve downloads it into `~/.cache/tamserve`, so that run needs an internet connection. EdgeTAM is 54 MB. The download is pinned to one version and verified before any of it is loaded.

### A live loop

tamserve does not open cameras, and it does not run a loop of its own. Your program reads frames however it likes and calls `engine.step()` once per round, with the newest frame from each camera exactly as the decoder gives it. This example uses OpenCV to read two network cameras:

```python
import threading

import cv2  # pip install opencv-python; any source of frames will do
from tamserve import Box, Engine, build_video_predictor

class Camera:
    """Reads one stream on a thread of its own and keeps its newest frame."""

    def __init__(self, url):
        self.stream, self.newest, self.arrived = cv2.VideoCapture(url), None, threading.Event()
        threading.Thread(target=self.read, daemon=True).start()

    def read(self):
        while True:
            ok, picture = self.stream.read()
            if not ok:
                break  # the stream has ended
            self.newest = cv2.cvtColor(picture, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)  # OpenCV gives BGR, the engine takes RGB
            self.arrived.set()

    def take(self):
        """Waits for a frame the loop has not seen yet, and returns it."""
        self.arrived.wait()
        self.arrived.clear()
        return self.newest

engine = Engine(build_video_predictor("cuda"))  # loads EdgeTAM onto the GPU
cameras = {"door": Camera("rtsp://door-camera/stream"), "yard": Camera("rtsp://yard-camera/stream")}

# What to track and where it is in the first frame: a box as (left, top, right, bottom), in pixels.
# In a real system this comes from a detector, or from someone drawing on the picture.
start = {"door": {"courier": Box(410, 120, 560, 480)}}

while True:
    # 1. Take the newest frame from each camera.
    frames = {name: camera.take() for name, camera in cameras.items()}

    # 2. One call tracks every object in every one of those frames.
    masks = engine.step(frames, start)
    start = None  # the box was only needed once; from here on the engine tracks the courier by itself

    # 3. Use the answer. masks["door"]["courier"] is True on the courier's pixels and False everywhere else.
    for camera_name, objects in masks.items():
        for object_name, mask in objects.items():
            print(camera_name, object_name, "covers", int(mask.sum()), "pixels")
```

Each call to `step()` takes one frame per camera and returns when the masks for those frames are ready. The engine remembers what it is tracking between calls, which is why the box is passed only once. Camera names and object names are yours to choose.

The frames go in exactly as the decoder gives them. The engine uploads them and resizes them on the GPU, which takes about half a millisecond a frame where resizing on the CPU takes 16. The `Camera` class is there for speed too: with a thread per camera, the next round's frames are decoded while the GPU tracks this one. And because a camera keeps only its newest frame, a loop that falls behind skips frames and does not lag. The engine tracks from whatever frame it is given and does not need to see every one.

How fast can the loop go? On an RTX 4090 with the compiled engine, eight 720p cameras and one object each, a loop like this one tracks 273 frames a second from video to masks, which is 34 for every camera. With 1080p cameras it is 238.

### Pointing at things

To start tracking something, you give it a name and point at it in the current frame. There are three ways to point. All of them use the frame's own pixel coordinates, with x counted from the left edge and y from the top.

| prompt | what it is |
|---|---|
| `Box(left, top, right, bottom)` | A rectangle around the thing. This is the most reliable, and it is what a detector gives you. |
| `Clicks([(x, y), ...])` | One or more points on the thing, as from a mouse. A second list of 1s and 0s can mark each point as on the thing (1) or deliberately off it (0). |
| a mask | A True/False array the size of the frame, if you already have the outline from somewhere else. |

### The four things you can do

**Start tracking something.** Pass its name and where it is, together with the frame it is in. You do this once. Everything already being tracked carries on undisturbed.

```python
engine.step(frames, {"yard": {"dog": Box(300, 380, 420, 470)}})
```

**Stop tracking something.**

```python
engine.drop("door", "courier")  # just the courier
engine.drop("door")             # everything on the door camera
```

**Fix a track that has gone wrong.** Now and then an outline drifts. It slides onto the wrong person, or keeps only half of the object. Point at the object again under the same name, exactly as you did to start it. Tracking begins afresh from the new box, and the old, mistaken history is thrown away.

```python
engine.step(frames, {"door": {"courier": Box(455, 130, 600, 500)}})  # same name, new box
```

**Start something you noticed in the frame you just processed.** `step()` moves every tracked object forward by one frame. Suppose a detector looked at the frame you just passed in and found a dog. Calling `step()` again with that same frame would move everything else forward twice. `add()` starts the dog on that frame and leaves the rest alone.

```python
engine.add(frames, {"yard": {"dog": Box(300, 380, 420, 470)}})  # frames: the ones you just gave step()
```

### Following what you name

Everything above starts from someone pointing at the thing. A `Tracker` takes words instead. Give it a phrase, or several, and it finds every match on every camera, follows each one, picks up new ones as they appear and lets go of those that leave.

One live camera on one RTX 4090. The words are set while it runs, and nobody points at anything. Watch the 17-second clip, read how it was recorded, or try it in Colab.

```python
from tamserve import Engine, Tracker, build_video_predictor

engine = Engine(build_video_predictor("cuda", "sam2.1-large"), compile=True)
tracker = Tracker(engine, {"door": ["person", "package"], "yard": "dog"})  # loads SAM 3, the model that finds things

while True:
    frames = {name: camera.take() for name, camera in cameras.items()}  # as in the live loop above
    masks = tracker.step(frames)
    # masks["door"] is {1: mask, 2: mask, 3: mask}: one mask for everything found on the door camera
    # tracker.names("door") is {1: "person", 2: "person", 3: "package"}: what each of them is
```

For the same phrase on every camera, `Tracker(engine, "dog")` is enough. Each thing gets a number, counted from 1 on each camera, and keeps it for as long as it is followed.

It works by pairing two models. SAM 3 is Meta's model that outlines whatever you name. It is accurate and slow: one look at one frame takes about 65 ms on an RTX 4090. The model inside the engine cannot find anything by itself, but it follows what it is given far more cheaply, a few ms a frame with EdgeTAM and a few tens with SAM 2.1 large. So SAM 3 looks at each camera once every three frames, the engine follows what it found in between, and the looks are spread out so that they never all land in the same round.

## dedsxc/mcp-frigate (https://github.com/dedsxc/mcp-frigate)
Description: Unofficial mcp-frigate to interact with https://github.com/blakeblackshear/frigate 
Homepage: -
Language: Python; license: none; created 2026-01-18; last push 2026-11-19
Latest release: frigate-mcp-0.1.0 (2026-11-02)
README (start):
# Frigate MCP Server

A [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server for [Frigate NVR](https://frigate.video/), enabling AI assistants to interact with your Frigate security camera system.

[](https://www.python.org/downloads/)
[](LICENSE)

## 🌟 Features

- **Camera Management**: List and monitor all configured cameras
- **Event Detection**: Query detection events with filtering by camera, object type, and time
- **Live Snapshots**: Get current or historical camera snapshots
- **Recordings**: Access recording summaries and segments
- **System Stats**: Monitor Frigate performance, detector speed, and camera FPS
- **Configuration**: Retrieve complete Frigate configuration

## 📋 Prerequisites

- Python 3.10 or higher
- A running [Frigate NVR](https://frigate.video/) instance
- Access to the Frigate HTTP API

## 🚀 Installation

### 1. Clone the repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/frigate-mcp.git
cd frigate-mcp
```

### 2. Create a virtual environment

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate  # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
```

### 3. Install dependencies

```bash
pip install -e .
```

### 4. Configure environment

Create a `.env` file in the project root:

```bash
# Required: URL of your Frigate instance
FRIGATE_FRIGATE_URL=http://localhost:5000

# Optional: API key if authentication is required
# FRIGATE_API_KEY=your_secret_key_here

# Optional: HTTP timeout in seconds (default: 30)
# FRIGATE_TIMEOUT=30
```

## 🔧 Configuration

The server uses environment variables for configuration. You can set them in:

1. **`.env` file** (recommended for development)
2. **Environment variables** (recommended for production)

### Configuration Options

| Variable              | Description                    | Default                 | Required |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------ | ----------------------- | -------- |
| `FRIGATE_FRIGATE_URL` | Base URL of Frigate instance   | `http://localhost:5000` | No       |
| `FRIGATE_API_KEY`     | API key for authentication     | None                    | No       |
| `FRIGATE_TIMEOUT`     | HTTP request timeout (seconds) | `30`                    | No       |
| `FRIGATE_SERVER_HOST` | Server host for SSE/HTTP modes | `0.0.0.0`               | No       |
| `FRIGATE_SERVER_PORT` | Server port for SSE/HTTP modes | `8000`                  | No       |

### Example Configurations

**Local Frigate instance:**
```bash
FRIGATE_FRIGATE_URL=http://localhost:5000
```

**Remote Frigate with authentication:**
```bash
FRIGATE_FRIGATE_URL=http://192.168.1.100:5000
FRIGATE_API_KEY=your_secret_key
FRIGATE_TIMEOUT=60
```

## 🎯 Usage

The server supports three operational modes:

### 1. STDIO Mode (Default)

For direct integration with MCP clients like Claude Desktop:

```bash
python -m frigate_mcp.server
# or
frigate-mcp
```

### 2. SSE Mode (Server-Sent Events)

For web-based clients with real-time updates:

```bash
frigate-mcp-sse
```

The server will start at `http://localhost:8000/sse` (configurable via environment variables).

**Features:**
- Real-time event streaming
- WebSocket-like experience over HTTP
- Easy to debug in browser dev tools
- Compatible with web applications

### 3. HTTP Mode (REST API)

For production deployments and API access:

**STDIO Mode** (for MCP clients):

```bash
python -m frigate_mcp.server
```

**SSE Mode** (for web clients):

```bash
frigate-mcp-sse
```

**HTTP Mode** (for REST API):

```bash
frigate-mcp-http
```

### Integrating with MCP Clients

#### Claude Desktop (STDIO Mode)
### Testing the Connection

Run the included test script to verify your Frigate connection:

```bash
python test_connection.py
```

Expected output:
```
============================================================
Frigate MCP Server - Connection Test
============================================================

🔧 Frigate Configuration:
   URL: http://localhost:5000
   API URL: http://localhost:5000/api
   Timeout: 30s

📹 Testing /api/config (cameras)...
   ✅ Found 1 camera(s)
      - front_door: enabled

📊 Testing /api/stats...
   ✅ Frigate version: 0.16.3
   ✅ Detectors: ['coral']
   ✅ Active cameras: ['front_door']
...
```

### Running the MCP Server

Start the server in stdio mode (for MCP clients):

```bash
python -m frigate_mcp.server
```

#### Claude Desktop (STDIO Mode)

Add to your MCP client configuration (e.g., Claude Desktop `config.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "frigate": {
      "command": "/path/to/frigate-mcp/.venv/bin/python",
      "args": ["-m", "frigate_mcp.server"],
      "env": {
        "FRIGATE_FRIGATE_URL": "http://localhost:5000"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

#### Web Clients (SSE Mode)

Connect to the SSE endpoint for real-time updates:

```javascript
const eventSource = new EventSource('http://localhost:8000/sse');

eventSource.onmessage = (event) => {
  const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
  console.log('Received:', data);
};
```

#### REST API (HTTP Mode)

Make standard HTTP requests:

```bash
# Get cameras
curl http://localhost:8000/tools/get_cameras

# Get events
curl http://localhost:8000/tools/get_events?limit=5

# Get stats
curl http://localhost:8000/tools/get_stats
```

Or use any HTTP client:

```python
import requests

response = requests.post(
    'http://localhost:8000/tools/get_events',
    json={'camera': 'front_door', 'limit': 10}
)
print(response.json())   "frigate": {
      "command": "/path/to/frigate-mcp/.venv/bin/python",
      "args": ["-m", "frigate_mcp.server"],
      "env": {
        "FRIGATE_FRIGATE_URL": "http://localhost:5000"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## 🛠️ Available Tools

The server provides 7 MCP tools for interacting with Frigate:

### 1. `get_cameras()`

List all configured cameras with their status and properties.

**Returns:**
```json
[
  {
    "name": "front_door",
    "enabled": true,
    "width": 1920,
    "height": 1080,
    "fps": 5
  }
]
```

### 2. `get_events(camera, label, limit)`

Get recent detection events with optional filtering.

**Parameters:**
- `camera` (optional): Filter by camera name
- `label` (optional): Filter by object type (`person`, `car`, `dog`, etc.)
- `limit` (default: 10): Maximum events to return (1-100)

**Example:**
```python
get_events(camera="front_door", label="person", limit=5)
```

**Returns:**
```json
[
  {
    "id": "1234567890.123456-abcdef",
    "camera": "front_door",
    "label": "person",
    "start_time": 1704067200.5,
    "end_time": 1704067205.8,
    "has_clip": true,
    "has_snapshot": true,
    "zones": ["entrance"],
    "thumbnail": "http://localhost:5000/api/events/1234.../thumbnail.jpg"
  }
]
```

### 3. `get_stats()`

Get Frigate system statistics and performance metrics.

**Returns:**
```json
{
  "service": {
    "uptime": 86400,
    "version": "0.16.3",
    "storage": {...}
  },
  "detectors": {
    "coral": {
      "inference_speed": 8.5,
      "detection_start": 1704067200.0
    }
  },
  "cameras": {
    "front_door": {
      "camera_fps": 5.0,
      "process_fps": 5.0,
      "detection_fps": 1.2
    }
  }
}
```

### 4. `get_event_details(event_id)`

Get comprehensive details about a specific event.

**Parameters:**
- `event_id`: Unique event identifier

**Returns:**
```json
{
  "id": "1234567890.123456-abcdef",
  "camera": "front_door",
  "label": "person",
  "start_time": 1704067200.5,
  "end_time": 1704067205.8,
  "duration": 5.3,
  "score": 0.87,
  "zones": ["entrance"],
  "has_clip": true,
  "has_snapshot": true,
  "media": {
    "thumbnail": "http://localhost:5000/api/events/.../thumbnail.jpg",
    "snapshot": "http://localhost:5000/api/events/.../snapshot.jpg",
    "clip": "http://localhost:5000/api/events/.../clip.mp4"
  }
}
```

### 5. `get_snapshot(camera, timestamp)`

Get a snapshot URL from a specific camera.

**Parameters:**
- `camera`: Camera name
- `timestamp` (optional): Unix timestamp for historical snapshot

**Returns:**
```json
{
```

# [CVPR2025] Segment Any Motion in Videos
**[Project Page](https://motion-seg.github.io/) | [Arxiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22268)**

[Nan Huang](https://github.com/nnanhuang)1,2, 
[Wenzhao Zheng](https://wzzheng.net/)1, 
[Chenfeng Xu](https://www.chenfengx.com/)1, 
[Kurt Keutzer](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~keutzer/)1,

[Angjoo Kanazawa](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~kanazawa/)1,[Qianqian Wang](https://qianqianwang68.github.io/)1

1UC Berkeley      2Peking University

Overview of Our Pipeline. We take 2D tracks and depth maps generated by off-the-shelf models as input, which are then
processed by a motion encoder to capture motion patterns, producing featured tracks. Next, we use tracks decoder that integrates DINO
feature to decode the featured tracks by decoupling motion and semantic information and ultimately obtain the dynamic trajectories(a).
Finally, using SAM2, we group dynamic tracks belonging to the same object and generate fine-grained moving object masks(b).

```bash
conda create -n seg python=3.12.4
conda activate seg
```

tamserve: results

Every measurement behind the README, with the command that produces it. All on one machine: an RTX 4090 (24 GB), an AMD EPYC 9354 limited to 8.8 cores, PyTorch 2.15 with CUDA 13.2, Python 3.11, bf16 autocast (how these models normally run on a GPU), EdgeTAM at commit 7711e01. How the engine works is in how-it-works.md.

"Stock" is the tracker in Meta's EdgeTAM repository, used as it comes: Meta's SAM 2 video predictor as it stood in late 2024, which also runs the SAM 2.1 models. Meta's separate SAM 2 repository has since changed its predictor (it can add objects mid-video and has its own compiled mode); SAM 2.1 is measured against that newer code too, in its own section. "Compiled" stock is its modules compiled the way Meta's vos_optimized mode compiles SAM 2 (EdgeTAM's repository ships no compiled mode), in torch.compile's max-autotune mode, with the one compiler fix the engine also uses (see Compiling); without that fix compiled stock ran at 126 frames/s instead of 186. The models' optional step that fills pinhole gaps in masks needs a CUDA extension built at install time; it is not built here, so neither stock nor tamserve applies it.

Throughput

bench/throughput.py. Synthetic 640x360 frames already on the GPU (cost depends on tensor shapes, not on what the pixels show), one object per camera, every object's memory full. Frames per second are summed over cameras.

Against stock's strongest setup

Stock runs one compiled process per camera, sharing the GPU through NVIDIA MPS, which lets the processes' work overlap on the GPU. The engine is one compiled process (Engine(compile=True)). Both are measured by the same code: a worker process runs for a 20-second window after a 10-second lead-in, synchronises with the GPU after every frame (stock) or step (engine), and counts the frames it finishes and the time they took. Stock's frames with a memory that is still filling, at the start of each pass over its video, are left out because they are cheaper.

python bench/throughput.py --arms procs-compiled --procs 1,2,4,8                    # stock
python bench/throughput.py --arms engine-procs --procs 1 --sizes 1,2,4,8,16,32,64   # tamserve
cameras	stock, frames/s	tamserve, frames/s		stock GPU / host memory	tamserve GPU / host memory
1	177	219	1.24x	1.1 / 2.6 GB	1.1 / 3.2 GB
2	258	286	1.11x	2.2 / 5.2 GB	1.3 / 3.2 GB
4	294	333	1.13x	4.3 / 10.5 GB	1.6 / 3.2 GB
8	280	323	1.15x	8.6 / 21.1 GB	2.2 / 3.2 GB
16		322			2.9 / 3.2 GB
32		319			3.3 / 3.2 GB
64		321			5.7 / 3.2 GB

GPU memory is what nvidia-smi reports in the middle of the window. Each stock process holds its 64-frame video on the GPU (0.75 GB), which is subtracted here. Stock was not run past 8 processes: 16 did not start on this host, whose container limits threads, and would need 17 GB of GPU memory before any video. Two earlier runs of each side landed within 4% of these: stock at 177 to 178, 259 to 260, 297 to 300 and 282 to 289, the engine at 217, 283, 331 and 322.

The engine copies every mask to the CPU in these numbers and stock leaves its masks on the GPU. With --gpu-masks the engine does the same and gains about 1% (220, 287, 332, 325, 320, 323 and 326 frames/s, measured on the build just before the last code review, when the engine's column read 217, 283, 331, 322, 320, 319 and 326).

One process, median step

The same engine measured inside one process, as the median of 30 steps, with peak GPU memory actually allocated. The uncompiled engine and stock on one camera are measured the same way. This table, the two after it, start-up and memory were measured on the build just before the last code review; the like-for-like and accuracy tables were measured again after it.

python bench/throughput.py --arms stock-eager,stock-compiled,engine-eager,engine-compiled --sizes 1,2,4,8,16,32,64
python bench/throughput.py --arms engine-compiled --engine-mode default --sizes 1,2,4,8,16,32,64
cameras	1	2	4	8	16	32	64
stock, uncompiled	57						
stock, compiled	186						
tamserve, uncompiled	55	109	212	207	195	193	186
tamserve, compile="default"	115	233	323	315	315	317	316
tamserve, compile=True	217	291	350	339	337	332	328
peak GPU memory, compile=True	0.3 GB	0.4 GB	0.6 GB	1.1 GB	1.5 GB	2.4 GB	4.6 GB

A quarter of the memory at 64 cameras is the benchmark's own frames (8 per camera). When steps are queued without waiting for each one's masks (gpu_masks=True, bench/engine_profile.py --gpu-masks), the engine reaches 255, 320, 354, 343 and 343 frames/s at 1 to 16 cameras.

The compiled engine at 1, 2, 4, 8 and 64 cameras, frames/s, in the order the changes were made. None of them changes a mask: uncompiled, one camera is still bit-identical to stock after all of them.

Start-up

Time until the engine is ready, from ready_s in bench/throughput.py. "First time" is with PyTorch's on-disk caches empty (TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR and TRITON_CACHE_DIR pointed at an empty folder).

Engine(compile=True)	1,190 s	about 95 s
Engine(compile="default")	164 s	45 to 75 s
uncompiled	2 s	2 s

The engine compiles five batch sizes, each for every memory length an object passes through, so that nothing compiles later; stock compiles one.

Accuracy
The bar: stock against itself

bench/noise_floor.py, DAVIS 2017 validation, 30 videos, 61 objects. How much stock's own masks change when nothing about the model changes:

stock against stock	mean overlap (IoU)	worst 1% of frames	lost objects
the same run twice	1.000	1.000	0
an object tracked alone, then next to the video's other objects	0.990	0.40	0
bf16, then fp32	0.983	0.24	0

Against the hand-drawn masks the two middle runs score 0.7988 and 0.7991: stock moves by 0.0002 from batch size alone, and single objects by up to 0.02. That is rounding, and it is the size of change batching is allowed to make.

The engine against stock

bench/accuracy.py (--compile best for the compiled engine). The 30 DAVIS videos are cameras that join 3 frames apart and leave when their video ends, so every step mixes objects that are starting, filling their memory, and in steady state: 10.7 cameras at once on average, 26 at most. Stock tracks each video on its own. Accuracy is mean overlap with the hand-drawn masks, averaged over videos. "Lost" counts frames where stock had an object and the engine did not; "extra" the reverse.

model	stock	tamserve	change	videos better / worse	lost / extra	overlap with stock's masks
EdgeTAM	0.8686	0.8684	-0.0002	14 / 16	0 / 2	0.988
EdgeTAM, compile=True	0.8686	0.8685	-0.0002	14 / 16	0 / 0	0.987

SAM 2.1 large	0.8919	0.8918	-0.0001	18 / 12	0 / 1	0.996

The extra frames are all in one video (kite-surf), where stock drops a small object for a frame or two and the engine keeps it. Compiled results are not repeatable to the last digit from one build to the next: an earlier build of the compiled EdgeTAM engine scored 0.8689 (+0.0002, 17 videos better, 13 worse), and of SAM 2.1 tiny 0.8805. The largest single-video changes are in the videos where stock varies most against itself: -0.019 (EdgeTAM, paragliding-launch) and -0.009 (SAM 2.1 small, pigs), which is most of that model's -0.0004.

Bit for bit

pytest (tests/test_engine.py): with Engine(exact=True) one camera gives masks identical to stock's on every frame, on the CPU and the GPU, for EdgeTAM and SAM 2.1 tiny, for mask, box and click prompts. 35 tests pass on a machine with two GPUs; 27 run without one.

Raw frames

Everything above feeds the engine frames resized on the CPU by prepare(), exactly as stock resizes them. A frame handed to step() as decoded is resized by the engine on the GPU instead, and a pixel can then differ from stock's by 1 (bench/accuracy.py --frames raw):

Against cameras

In the throughput tables above: 2.2 GB of GPU memory and 3.2 GB of host memory for 8 cameras in one process, against 8.6 GB and 21.2 GB for eight stock processes.

SAM 2.1

SAM 2.1 keeps 4,096 memory tokens per frame where EdgeTAM keeps 512, so memory attention is most of a step (6 of 11 ms per camera for SAM 2.1 tiny) and the GPU is the limit from one camera on. Batching cameras cannot raise its frame rate; the engine's lead over stock is what removing the waits and the per-frame position encodings is worth.

SAM 2.1 tiny, measured exactly as EdgeTAM above (--model sam2.1-tiny). Compiled, one process per camera for stock, one process for the engine:

Against Meta's current SAM 2 code

The tracker in EdgeTAM's repository is a late-2024 copy of Meta's. Meta's own SAM 2 repository has moved on since: its tracker follows each object independently, can add an object after tracking has started, and has a compiled mode (vos_optimized). So SAM 2.1 was measured again against that code, the sam2 package at version 1.1.0, installed next to tamserve with uv pip install sam2 and selected in the benchmarks with --stock.

Four 10-second clips from Pexels, cut to 1280 x 720 and attached to the tamserve release; free to use under the Pexels licence. Originals: welder, cat, airport, office. The boxes say where each object is in the first frame; in a real system they come from a detector or a click.

import urllib.request
import cv2
import numpy as np
CLIPS = {  # Pexels id -> {object: (left, top, right, bottom) on the first frame}
    "14314645": {"welder": (228, 138, 787, 714)},
    "7727397": {"cat": (620, 212, 1052, 713)},
    "856984": {"plane": (536, 309, 799, 410), "marshaller": (1073, 571, 1120, 631)},
    "6914684": {"person 1": (3, 282, 388, 631), "person 2": (480, 190, 736, 558), "person 3": (877, 186, 1279, 573)},
}
BASE = "https://github.com/aryamandarda/tamserve/releases/download/v0.2.0/"
def frames_of(pexels_id):
    """The clip's frames as 1280 x 720 RGB arrays, as a camera would send them."""
    path = f"/tmp/{pexels_id}.mp4"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{BASE}{pexels_id}.mp4", path)
    capture, frames = cv2.VideoCapture(path), []
    while (frame := capture.read())[0]:
        frames.append(cv2.cvtColor(frame[1], cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB))
    return frames
videos = {pexels_id: frames_of(pexels_id) for pexels_id in CLIPS}
print({pexels_id: len(frames) for pexels_id, frames in videos.items()})

One engine, one call per round: each round hands it the next frame of every camera and gets back every object's mask.

import time
from tamserve import Box, Engine, build_video_predictor

engine = Engine(build_video_predictor("cuda"))  # EdgeTAM. Engine(..., compile=True) is faster, after a long first compile.
masks = {pexels_id: [] for pexels_id in videos}
start = time.perf_counter()
for k in range(300):
    frames = {pexels_id: v[k] for pexels_id, v in videos.items() if k < len(v)}
    prompts = {pexels_id: {name: Box(*box) for name, box in CLIPS[pexels_id].items()} for pexels_id in frames} if k == 0 else None
    for pexels_id, objects in engine.step(frames, prompts).items():
        masks[pexels_id].append({name: m[::2, ::2].numpy() for name, m in objects.items()})  # half size, for drawing
took = time.perf_counter() - start
n = sum(len(m) for m in masks.values())
print(f"{n} frames from {len(videos)} cameras, {sum(map(len, CLIPS.values()))} objects, in {took:.1f} s: "
      f"{n / took:.0f} frames/s on {torch.cuda.get_device_name()}")

        if k >= len(masks[pexels_id]):
            continue
        tile = cv2.resize(videos[pexels_id][k], (640, 360), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32)
        for j, m in enumerate(masks[pexels_id][k].values()):
            m = cv2.resize(m.astype(np.uint8), (640, 360), interpolation=cv2.INTER_NEAREST).astype(bool)
            tile[m] = tile[m] * 0.5 + np.array(COLORS[j % 3]) * 0.5
        y, x = divmod(t, 2)
        wall[y * 360:(y + 1) * 360, x * 640:(x + 1) * 640] = tile.astype(np.uint8)
    writer.stdin.write(wall.tobytes())
writer.stdin.close()
writer.wait()
Video("/tmp/wall.mp4", embed=True, width=960)

Frigate NVR™ - Realtime Object Detection for IP Cameras

[English] | 简体中文

A complete and local NVR designed for Home Assistant with AI object detection. Uses OpenCV and Tensorflow to perform realtime object detection locally for IP cameras.

Use of a GPU or AI accelerator is highly recommended. AI accelerators will outperform even the best CPUs with very little overhead. See Frigate's supported object detectors.

Tight integration with Home Assistant via a custom component
Designed to minimize resource use and maximize performance by only looking for objects when and where it is necessary
Leverages multiprocessing heavily with an emphasis on realtime over processing every frame
Uses a very low overhead motion detection to determine where to run object detection
Object detection with TensorFlow runs in separate processes for maximum FPS
Communicates over MQTT for easy integration into other systems
Records video with retention settings based on detected objects
24/7 recording
Re-streaming via RTSP to reduce the number of connections to your camera
WebRTC & MSE support for low-latency live view

## Frigate NVR
URL: https://frigate.video/
Description: NVR with realtime local object detection for IP cameras

Azimuth

Close Menu
Monitor your security cameras with locally processed AI

Frigate is an open source NVR built around real-time AI object detection. All processing is performed locally on your own hardware, and your camera feeds never leave your home.

Get access to custom models designed specifically for Frigate with Frigate+.

Learn about Frigate+
Features

The most popular NVR for privacy focused home automation enthusiasts. See why.

Reduce false positives with local object detection

Traditional NVRs can require hours of fine tuning to reduce false positive rates because they rely on simple motion detection. By offloading object detection to a supported AI accelerator, even modest hardware can run advanced analysis to determine if the motion is actually a person, car, or other object of interest. With Frigate's local processing, there is no need to pay for your personal camera footage to be sent to the cloud for analysis.

Stop reviewing shadows and wind and start reviewing detections that matter

Let Frigate's AI scrub your video feeds for you. With a supported AI accelerator, Frigate can run 100+ object detections per second so it doesn't miss a single frame.

Fine tune your events and alerts with zones

Frigate tracks objects in real-time and can determine the exact moment a person starts walking up your front steps or when a car enters your driveway. Refine your notifications based on precise locations.

Integrate with Home Assistant and other automation platforms

Give your home eyes by integrating object detection into Home Assistant, OpenHab, NodeRed, or anything with MQTT support. Frigate integrates directly into Home Assistant's media browser, provides low latency camera entities, and exposes real-time sensors and switches to power automations and notifications to your heart's content.

Testimonials
